Today was surreal! Prince William's team asked me to work with him over the coming years on a project to end homelessness in the UK through his Foundation @homewardsuk ! This is part of a multi-year campaign that me and Prince William are embarking on to change the state of homelessness in the UK.

🥪 We started the day in a Pret A Manger in Bournemouth! We both put on aprons, made coffee's, sandwiches, and got to meet some of the incredible team members that are former refugees, former inmates and formerly homeless!

⚽️ We drove over to Bournemouth FC and met players from the Men's and Women's team who had come through the bounce back program and used football to change their lives. 

🎤 I was lucky enough to have a few moments to ask the future king some questions on his own personal motivations and how we manages his time! 

👩🏻‍💼 Myself and Prince William then hosted a business round table with a group of local business leaders about how they could work to hire more homeless individuals into their organisation! 

This is just the beginning of a big piece of work we're planning to do with Prince William, Homewards and the UK business community to help get homeless people (and former inmates) back into work, to up-skill them and to end homelessness for good!

🤯 Side note:

If you had told me as a kid, I would be spending the day with Prince William, the future King - I would never ever ever believed you. I grew up with a Nigerian mother and a english dad who both adore the royal family, one of my earliest memories is watching my mum and dad cry when Diana died. William has a wonderful way with people, and he was authentically kind both on and off camera today! Thank you to whatever force in the universe put me there today, I'm so grateful and a little confused. A day I'm sure I'll tell my kids about. 

If you're a business please do check out Homewards work! Together as a business community we can do a lot more to get all the talent we have in this country back to work! ❤️

What do you say to your family when you don’t know if you’ll ever see them again?

In February 2022, he told his wife and children the war had begun. Then he left as Russian forces advanced towards Kyiv, unsure what the coming hours would bring.

This is President Volodymyr Zelenskyy (zelenskyy_official) 

Before politics, he built a successful career in Ukrainian television as a writer, producer and performer, even portraying a president on screen. In 2019, he was elected President of Ukraine. Three years later, Russia launched its full-scale invasion.

Sitting down with him was surreal and an enormous responsibility. It was a rare chance to hear his account of the first hours of the war and the decisions that followed.

We discussed things like:

- How he found out Russia had invaded.
- Why he refused an offer to evacuate Kyiv.
- The 64km Russian military convoy advancing towards the capital.
- How Russian forces tried to capture a key airport.
- His account of discovering hundreds of bodies after Russian occupation.
- What he believes it will take to end the war.

But I also wanted to understand how he’d been coping.

One of my first questions was simply, “How are you doing?” His answer was: “It’s hard.”

He spoke about meeting parents whose children had been killed. Some, he explained, simply ask him for a hug.

And as he spoke, there were tears in his eyes.

Whatever your views on the war or the decisions made by those involved, this is a rare opportunity to hear his account of events that have changed millions of lives.

Because behind every map, every headline and every political decision, there are real people.

Out now on all platforms ❤️👊🏾

She said Yes 💍🥺

To say I was nervous is an understatement… i could feel my heart racing in my chest. She thought I was away in Europe - but I had snuck into Morocco on Christmas Day where she was on holiday with her family - I asked her mother and father if I could ask her to marry me - then had to build this big hut outside because a thunderstorm was forecast last minute 😅 - and then I stepped out and surprised her when she thought she was meeting her fam for dinner. 10 years ago, I didn’t really understand the concept of marriage as many of you know - I was definitely an “avoidant” - but when you meet the right person, a lot of things start to make a lot of sense ❤️

SOME NEWS 🚨 this year I’m joining @sharktankabc !!! 📺 🇺🇸 this was a dream of mine AND my mums...let me explain👇🏾

My nigerian mum raised 4 of us without being able to read or write herself, having left school when she was a child in Nigeria.

I struggled with school too - I wasn’t a smart kid and couldn’t pay attention, so I quickly realised the “traditional path” wasn’t going to work for someone like me

Then, when I was 12 years old, I discovered Dragons’ Den! 🐉

Me and my mum both fell in love with the show. Looking back, I think entrepreneurship offered us both hope - a path to a better life for people like us, who couldn’t pass tests in a classroom but were willing to work hard.

At 12 I would pause the TV and give my verdict, as if I was the 6th Dragon

By 16 I’d discovered Shark Tank and was starting my first (terrible) businesses

By 18 I was a university dropout with a start-up

And somehow, 9 years later, I ended up sitting in one of those Dragons’ Den chairs I used to shout at from our sofa

My mum has never fully gotten over it. 

When I call her today, 6 years later, the conversation is still 80% Dragons’ Den - her opinion on what I said, the businesses, what SHE would have done...

Btw, i’m genuinely not sure if she knows I have a podcast 😂 i don’t think she’s ever mentioned it 😅

But she knows Dragons’ Den, and that’s more than enough for her.

I know she’s always wanted me to do Shark Tank, so this phone call - telling her that day had come absolutely made my day, and hopefully her’s too!

I very much hope to do her proud + all of you that have supported me for the longest time... wish me luck!! 👊🏾❤️

@adamgrant is an organizational psychologist, bestselling author and professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania. He is widely known for studying how people think, work, collaborate and build relationships. His research explores what motivates people, how teams function, why some individuals succeed while others struggle, and how workplaces can become more productive and fulfilling. Through his work, he challenges conventional ideas about success, leadership and human behaviour.

Adam is the author of several bestselling books, including Give and Take, Originals, Option B (co-authored with Sheryl Sandberg), Think Again and Hidden Potential. His books explore topics such as generosity, creativity, rethinking beliefs, overcoming setbacks and developing human potential. His work combines psychological research with practical insights that people can apply to their careers, relationships and everyday decisions. He is also known for his TED Talks, podcast Rethinking and ability to make complex psychological concepts accessible to a broad audience.

In his work, Adam focuses on helping people become better thinkers, colleagues, leaders and friends. He examines how to recognise genuine generosity, challenge assumptions, give and receive feedback, and build stronger connections with others. His book Vibe explores the dynamics of relationships and how people connect with one another. By bringing together research and real-world examples, Adam encourages people to rethink how they approach work, friendships and personal growth.

If you want to know what determination looks like, meet Shabana Basij-Rasikh.
 
Shabana was six years old when the Taliban first seized power 30 years ago and banned girls in Afghanistan from attending school. Undeterred, she continued her education in secret schools across Kabul, then went on to graduate magna cum laude from Middlebury College in Vermont and earn a master’s degree in public policy from Oxford.
 
But Shabana didn’t stop at pursuing her own education. While still in college, she co-founded @sola.afghanistan, Afghanistan’s first boarding school for girls, which attracted students from nearly every province in the country.
 
When the Taliban returned to power in 2021, they shut girls out of the classroom once again. Yet Shabana fought to keep her school alive, leading the SOLA community’s evacuation to Rwanda.
 
In the years since, the Taliban have enacted a brutal campaign against women’s rights, barring them from universities, most jobs, traveling without a male relative, and even speaking and singing in public. But Shabana has not given up on her mission. SOLA continues to educate Afghan girls in exile from its campus in Rwanda, and it reaches girls in Afghanistan through online learning.
 
I’ve been honored to get to know Shabana through Pivotal’s Global Leaders initiative, which provides visionary changemakers with funds to support work they believe in, and I couldn’t think of a more important person to interview for International Day of the Girl. She knows exactly what’s at stake when girls are denied an education—and what’s possible when they can get one.
 
Read my Q&A with @sbasijrasikh at the link in my bio. #internationaldayofthegirl

Margaret Hamilton was an extraordinary woman. One of the first programmers on the Apollo mission, she helped Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin safely reach the moon, coined the term “software engineer,” and inspired countless other people to break barriers in STEM.
 
She was also a mom. And with the news of her passing, I find myself thinking about a story I once read about her:
 
Margaret sometimes brought her daughter Lauren to work at NASA. One night, Lauren pushed a button that made the system crash. Margaret immediately realized that an astronaut might inadvertently do the same thing, so she recommended adjusting the software. 
 
Margaret’s bosses ignored her advice. But during the very next mission, the astronauts made the exact same mistake her daughter did. “After that, they let me put the program change in,” she said.
 
What a powerful reminder of the unique perspectives that parents bring to the table. That breakthroughs and discovery can come from unexpected places. That all around us, unsung heroes are working quietly and faithfully to expand our idea of what’s possible.
 
Thank you, Margaret, for encouraging us all to soar.

One day, you might look back at your life and realise that the things you regret the most weren’t the mistakes you made, the opportunities you lost, or even the times you failed. They were the moments when you convinced yourself not to try.

The message you never sent. The idea you never started. The opportunity you turned down because you didn’t feel ready. The dream you quietly gave up on because you couldn’t handle the thought of people watching you fail.

And the scary part? You might never know what could have happened if you had just given yourself a chance.

We spend so much time trying to protect ourselves from disappointment that we end up protecting ourselves from possibilities, too. We want guarantees before we take the first step. We want to know that things will work out before we put ourselves out there. But life rarely gives you that kind of certainty.

Sometimes, you have to be the person who tries before they feel confident. Who starts before they feel qualified. Who takes a chance even when there’s a very real possibility that things might not go as planned.

Because failing at something you genuinely wanted will hurt, yes. But slowly watching yourself become someone who never even tries? That hurts in a different way.

You don’t need to have everything figured out today. You don’t need to be fearless. You just need to stop letting the possibility of things going wrong decide what you’re allowed to pursue.

Years from now, you deserve to look back and know that you gave yourself a real chance at the life you wanted.

Not everything will work out. Not every risk will pay off. But at least you’ll know that you didn’t let fear make all your decisions for you.

Ever noticed how you can spend an entire day being busy and still feel like you’ve accomplished absolutely nothing?

You wake up, open your laptop, check a few messages, start working on something, get distracted by a notification, watch a couple of reels, and suddenly remember that there were ten other things you wanted to finish. By the end of the day, you’re exhausted, but the one thing that actually mattered is still incomplete.

The problem isn’t always that you lack discipline or motivation. Sometimes, you’re simply giving too many things a piece of yourself without giving anything your best.

Every time you interrupt what you’re doing to check something else, it becomes harder to get back into the same rhythm. You might be physically sitting at your desk, but mentally, you’re everywhere except where you need to be.

And the worst part? You start mistaking constant activity for real progress.

The people who get extraordinary things done aren’t necessarily the ones who work the longest hours. They’re often the ones who know how to protect their attention. They understand that meaningful progress requires being present long enough to think deeply, solve problems, and see things through.

So the next time you have something important to finish, try this: put your phone away, close the unnecessary tabs, and give yourself permission to work on just that one thing.

You don’t need to conquer your entire to-do list in the next hour. You just need to make genuine progress on what matters most.

i think one of the most important words every founder needs to delete from their dictionary is “cringe.”

because honestly, we were cringe at every stage of building figuring out 😂

when i started recording videos alone, with no professional setup, hiding cracks in the wall with books.

that was cringe.

when we started working out of my house, with 2-3 team members living together, sharing rooms and bathrooms.

that was cringe.

when we moved into a tiny office with barely any amenities or proper chairs.

cringe again.

when we finally got a bigger office, grew too fast, ran out of space and started sitting on the floor to work.

even more cringe 😂

but here’s what i’ve realised.

what looked cringe to the world was progress to us.

we weren’t trying to look like a successful company.

we were trying to become one.

and there’s a massive difference.

we didn’t have the money, the setup, the resources or the experience.

but we had this stupid, almost delusional belief that we could build something extraordinary.

and we were okay looking stupid while figuring out how.

today, linkedin has recognised us among the top startups of 2026.

20 million subscribers. one of the biggest podcasts in the world. an incredible team, beautiful offices, cameras, lights, everything we once wished we had.

and the funniest part?

i’m 100% sure we’re still doing things today that people find cringe.

and 5 years from now, we’ll probably look back and laugh at ourselves too.

GOOD.

because i never want us to become so successful that we become afraid of looking stupid again.

so if you’re building something right now from your bedroom, your parents’ house, a tiny office, with borrowed equipment, with 2 people who believe in your crazy idea

please don’t waste your energy trying to look cool.

being cringe is temporary. not trying because you’re afraid of being cringe can cost you your entire dream.

thank you @linkedin_in for this recognition. and thank you to every single person who’s been part of this very messy, very embarrassing, very beautiful journey.

we’re still figuring out.

and hopefully, we’ll always be a little cringe. ❤️

Today I turn 80.

The years have brought many chapters, many faces, many beginnings and endings. Through all of them, the deeper question has remained the same: What is it that changes, and what is it that remains?

I feel immense gratitude for this life, for the people who have shared it with me, and for the mystery that continues to reveal itself in every moment.

The journey continues.

The roles we carry matter. They hold our work, responsibilities, relationships, and much of the life we have built. Over time, though, they can become so familiar that they begin to feel inseparable from who we are.

In Awakening in the Final Chapter, Deepak turns toward what remains beneath those changing identities: the awareness that has been present through every chapter of life.
